messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 78
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Potter
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 60

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Mirror Checking: keep checking mirrors, Checking Locks: repeatedly check locks, doors, or windows, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to, Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mabel is a seventy-eight-year-old potter who has lived alone since her husband died twelve years ago. She spends most of her days in the small studio she built onto the back of her house, shaping clay on the wheel and firing pieces in the kiln that hums beside the garden. It was there, in that studio, that the assault happened. A man she did not know forced open the side door just after dusk. He demanded money. When she told him there was none, he struck her twice across the face and pushed her to the floor. He left without taking anything, but Mabel lay on the cold concrete for what felt like hours before she could stand.

In the weeks afterward, she began to notice that she could not stop checking the locks. Every time she walked past the front door, she had to touch the deadbolt to be sure it was fastened. She would check the windows three or four times before bed, then again in the middle of the night when she woke with her heart pounding. Sometimes she found herself staring into the mirror in the hallway, not to see her own face but to scan the reflection behind her—to make sure there was no one standing in the doorway. She had come to believe that the world was a dangerous place, that danger could appear without warning, and that she had to be constantly ready. What frightened her most was the way her body kept reacting: her hands would shake even when she was sitting safely in her kitchen, her stomach would knot at a sudden creak of the floorboards, and she could not relax no matter how many times she told herself she was alone.

The memory of that evening forced its way into her mind without permission. She would be working a lump of clay on the wheel, the rhythmic pressure of her palms grounding her, and then suddenly she would see the man’s face, the way his eyes had locked onto hers, and she would feel the impact of his fist as if it were happening right now. The memories were mostly pictures—the angle of the light, the scuff of his boot on the tile, the smear of blood on her palm when she touched her mouth. She tried hard not to think about the event, telling herself that if she went over it again she would not be able to handle it, that she would fall apart entirely. But the images came anyway, mostly during the quiet of her studio or in the dead hours of the night.

The consequences of her vigilance crept into her daily life. She stopped working in the studio after four in the afternoon, because the fading light made her feel exposed. When she did throw clay, she kept the studio door locked from the inside, and every few minutes she would stop and listen for footsteps, for the click of a latch. Her production slowed, and she began to turn down commissions. Her daughter, who lived three hours away, noticed that Mabel no longer answered the phone after dark. When she visited, she found that Mabel had removed the mirror from the studio because she kept catching a glimpse of her own reflection and spinning around in fear.

What finally brought Mabel to seek help was a night when she woke to the sound of her own scream. She had been dreaming that the man was back, that she was on the floor again, unable to move. In the dream she had tried to call out but no sound came. She woke sitting up, gasping, her hands gripping the sheets so tightly that her knuckles ached. She turned on every light in the house and checked every lock twice, then sat in the kitchen until dawn, certain that she was still in danger even though she knew logically that the house was empty. The next morning she called her daughter, who drove down that weekend and helped her find a therapist. Mabel is afraid that she will never feel safe again, that her work—the only thing that has felt like her own since her husband died—will be taken from her by the fear. But she is also hoping that maybe, if she can tell someone the story in full and not push it away, the images will stop feeling like they are happening now, and she will be able to sit at her wheel without looking over her shoulder.
